Welcome to All Things Photonics, a podcast about the physical science of light driving
scientific innovation in the 21st century. I'm Joel Williams, Associate Editor at Photonics
Media. Join us as we explore the latest trends in optics, lasers, microscopy, and spectroscopy.
Each episode you'll hear from leading voices from across the photonics landscape,
brought to you by Photonics Media.
It wouldn't be accurate to classify the hobby of laser collecting as burgeoning,
and there are reasons for that. Compare lasers to postage stamps. Lasers are sizable space
occupiers. Where an argon-ion laser may be hard-pressed to fit neatly on a side table,
stamps fold neatly into an album that can be tucked away on a bookshelf.
Give or take, a high-power semiconductor laser is a $12,000 investment. These days,
a newly-issued Forever stamp is about 58 cents. And then, of course, there's the issue of safety.
A mishap with a laser is apt to bring consequences.
Beyond a paper cut. With all this in mind, it was still a surprise to learn that the laser collecting
community is really a small one. And for this reason, it didn't take us long at all, you might
say the process was ultra-fast, to be able to put our finger on the pulse of this community.
A collector here and an enthusiast there is very much the status quo. The lack of prominent
collectors makes the agglomerations of those who do proclaim their love of the light source that
much more impressive. Today on All Things Photonics, we introduce you to one of these collectors,
Bob Hess. His name is Bob Hess. And to your laser pointer and cat toy, Bob Hess raises you his
collection of 500 lasers and countless other laser materials and holograms. The time is right for us
to be speaking with Hess. After decades of confining his growing stock of lasers to his
house and personal storage spaces, we touch a bit on the floor plan of Hess' home in our interview.
Hess has launched an exhibit called Vintage Lasers and Holograms. The celebration of the
first 60 years of the laser industry features nearly 200 lasers and holograms. The exhibition
is a celebration of Hess' own journey, from self-described starving artist to a long-standing
member of the global community of holographers. Hess' day job as the director of holography at
Satori Optics ties in nicely with the hobby that takes on a central theme of our interview.
Our conversation begins with a trip back in time, as we begin our own quest not to own 500 lasers,
but to understand how someone does.
Holography at Satori Optics, Bob Hess, with news editor Jake Saltzman.
I've always liked old things. I tend to not throw things away, so that started the path.
I'm a laser technician, photonics technician, and a holographer. And for the first 15 years of my
life, I was a starving artist doing it, so I had to be creative and hang on to everything I could
and scrounge things.
In the mid-80s, I scrounged an old laser and hung on to it for a while, and it just kind of grew
from there. I'm also a single guy, so if you have space available, it gets filled with things like
that. Tell us about your collection. I'm not stretching the truth when I say one of the
world's leading collectors. You're able to have an exhibit, an exhibition on, and you certainly
have space and you use it. Tell us about the collection, what's in it, and how sizeable is it?
Well, it's pretty big. There's about 500 lasers in the collection now, probably another 500
related accessories, like power meters and orphan power supplies, that sort of thing, and
components like raw diodes or plasma tubes or things that actually go into the laser.
There's another 500 publications, another 600 or so holograms, because it's my
own career, plus the ones that I've collected over the years. So it's pretty big.
Some people have dogs, some people have cats, some people have raw diodes, I understand.
Tell us, I want you to set the scene for us if you can. I can't imagine you walk in and, you know,
there's the kitchen, there's the femtosecond laser, there's the bathroom, there's the eczema laser.
That can't be true, is it?
Pretty much it is. Well, I was in San Jose in a very small house when I started the collection,



so I was limited to small early lasers. But when I moved to Phoenix eight years ago,
I had much more space in the house I had to get. And so I stopped along the way and
picked up a bunch from Brian Bohan at Cambridge Lasers in Fremont. He had a bunch of old big ones.
And Bob Arkin at Holospectra had a bunch of big old ones I stopped and picked up.
And I've made a few trips around the country picking things up over the years.
So I pretty much filled up the house.
So you're a photonics guy, right?
In the living room, the garage is full, everything was full.
Yeah, I was going to say the garage has to be probably the first to go, so to speak.
You're a photonics technician, you're a lasers guy, but lasers aren't toys. They're immensely
interesting, but they're not toys. They're expensive, industrial in many cases, items.
So we found a simple motivation to build it bigger with regards to your collection.
What's been the motivation to collect these materials, components, and devices?
Well, originally, I had a few old lasers from the 80s. But then around 2006,
I was in a position where I thought, I need a new hobby. So I started to collect holograms,
but I couldn't really find old holograms. And I started running into old lasers. And I
ran into one that was from 1962, a pulsed ruby laser that was still operational.
So I thought, I'm going to put my hands on that and make a few holograms with it.
And I experienced what they did back then with a basic laser. And then I'll find the museum or
wherever it should be after I play with it for a few years. So I did that for a couple of years.
And then it was around 2009, the 50th anniversary of the laser was looming in 2010. So I thought,
well, I'll see how old this one is and did some research.
And I also wanted to identify the original laser that was used by Leith and Eupatinix to make a new laser.



And I also wanted to identify the original laser that was used by Leith and Eupatinix to make the first hologram.

They're the equipment.

And laser levels.

There's distance measurement lasers.
There's telescope alignment lasers.

These are all things that people buy as products.

They're going to buy products and interact with the actual beam itself.
There's also laser light show projectors and holiday lighting things now that are projecting laser beams.

You know, now there's...
There's videos on YouTube of rust removal lasers that are really dramatic.
Can't wait to get my hands on one of those and build a demonstration so you can actually demonstrate that happening.
Very dramatic.
And there's also holography.
A big application of lasers.

Since Goldfinger's laser.

They've always been prevented from actually seeing the actual devices because of laser safety issues and all that, the high voltages and stuff.
So nobody ever really got to see under the cover of the laser.

Laser light safely.

It's enabled by the laser.

Pulsed portraits, animated holograms people enjoy seeing.

You have thousands of lasers and components combined.

There's so many of them.
I mean, I just love them.
They're like old cars to me.
I don't think each one.

62 model 111 from Perkin Elmer Spectrophysics.

CW, Heaney.
It's the first one, old laser I bought in the mid 80s.
I bought the head because it had the model number 111.
And I thought that was cool.
And it was Perkin Elmer and Spectrophysics.
I thought that was, it's got to be special.
But I never, and I dragged it around, but I never looked it up or didn't know.
Really what it was until I started researching lasers, you know, more recently.

Another one is a mid 60s Carson Labs model 200 argon ion laser.
Super rare company that made.
Lasers in the, on the East coast.
And they were the first company to make an argon laser or an ion laser with a ceramic plasma tube.
And a special feature was this viewing port where you can see a little indicator that goes up and down as you adjust the mirror position.
And you've never seen that feature on any other laser since.
So it's a really special little features on lasers like that, that I really liked with the old ones.
And then a third one would be the 1978.
Model nine 50 CO2 laser from GTE, Sylvania.
I bought that from Dick Anderson in Ohio.
I was there in like 2017 rummaging through looking for old lasers, saw that.
Bought it because it had the adjuster that I don't have on another one.
And I took it home and I was at my mom's house and outside of Chicago.

From when I worked at Spectra physics, my first laser job in 1982 was building the old line of CO2 lasers from Sylvania.
The Spectra physics had bought and continued.
And so my first job was processing and building plasma tubes and refurbishing those heads.
So here it is, you know, 35 years later and I encounter one of my first laser tubes from my first job.
Reconnected with yourself.
Yeah.
Yeah.
It's just great.
And I found that out when I was at my mom's, you know, and she's in her nineties.
So it was a special thing.

Is there such a thing either globally or internationally?
